Syntactic Structure & Grammatical Form: Fixed two-part greeting formula: an independent gratitude expression followed by a stative well-being expression.
Figurative Meaning (Contextualized Defin: A culturally grounded greeting that acknowledges gratitude for the other person’s continued wellness and peaceful state.
Non-Idiomatic Equivalent (Plain, Neutral: I am thankful that you are well.
Usage Contexts: Greetings; family; community gatherings; classroom; workplace; ceremonial-adjacent daily speech
Cultural Origin or Historical Reference: An established Seneca greeting. Its literal components foreground thankfulness and well-being rather than merely marking contact, reflecting the social importance of reciprocal recognition.

Syntactic Structure & Grammatical Form: Fixed monomorphemic response particle functioning as a complete utterance.
Figurative Meaning (Contextualized Defin: Signals assent, acceptance, closure, blessing, or agreement; in some settings it carries the force of “amen” or “so be it.”
Non-Idiomatic Equivalent (Plain, Neutral: Yes; I agree; let it be so.
Usage Contexts: Daily decisions; meetings; family talk; public speaking; prayer or ceremonial conclusions
Cultural Origin or Historical Reference: Attested with the linked meanings “all right,” “amen,” and “so be it,” showing how one response particle spans everyday and solemn domains.

Figurative Meaning (Contextualized Defin: Encourages someone to begin, proceed, try, or act decisively.
Usage Contexts: Games; work; teaching; encouragement; playful challenges
Cultural Origin or Historical Reference: An attested action-launching expression glossed as “OK! Go for it!” It is useful for modeling directive force without a full lexical verb.

Syntactic Structure & Grammatical Form: Fixed emotive interjection; independent exclamatory utterance.
Figurative Meaning (Contextualized Defin: Expresses surprise, concern, admiration, frustration, or sympathetic alarm depending on intonation.
Usage Contexts: Family conversation; storytelling; humor; reacting to news; mild complaint
Cultural Origin or Historical Reference: Attested as a conventional exclamation. Its interpretation depends heavily on prosody and context, making it valuable for sentiment and pragmatic modeling.

Syntactic Structure & Grammatical Form: Fixed epistemic-response particle; may stand alone or modify an assertion.
Figurative Meaning (Contextualized Defin: Affirms that something is true, correct, or genuinely the case; it can also seek or signal confirmation.
Non-Idiomatic Equivalent (Plain, Neutral: That is true; really; that is right.
Usage Contexts: Question answering; confirmation; storytelling; correction; debate
Cultural Origin or Historical Reference: Attested with the meanings “that’s right” and “really.” It is a compact marker of evidential commitment and conversational alignment.

Syntactic Structure & Grammatical Form: Fixed deictic-closing formula used as a complete utterance.
Figurative Meaning (Contextualized Defin: Marks completion, identification, or conversational closure: the matter has reached its endpoint.
Non-Idiomatic Equivalent (Plain, Neutral: That is it; that is all.
Usage Contexts: Instructions; demonstrations; storytelling endings; task completion; conversation closing
Cultural Origin or Historical Reference: Attested as “that’s it.” It develops from a deictic element referring to what is there or what has just been established in discourse.

Syntactic Structure & Grammatical Form: Fixed discourse particle functioning independently or parenthetically.
Figurative Meaning (Contextualized Defin: Marks strong confirmation, insistence, or the speaker’s commitment that a statement is indeed true.
Usage Contexts: Narrative emphasis; argument; testimony; correction; public speaking
Cultural Origin or Historical Reference: Attested as “really, indeed, in fact.” It is important for modeling stance, speaker certainty, and information structure.

Syntactic Structure & Grammatical Form: Lexicalized intensifying adverbial expression used independently or before/after a focused assertion.
Figurative Meaning (Contextualized Defin: Strengthens a claim to mean that something is genuinely, completely, or unmistakably so.
Usage Contexts: Strong agreement; praise; complaint; storytelling; persuasive speech
Cultural Origin or Historical Reference: Attested as an expanded intensifier meaning “really, very much so.” Its fuller form carries greater pragmatic weight than an ordinary degree word.

Syntactic Structure & Grammatical Form: Fixed manner adverb used predicatively or as a discourse-level characterization.
Figurative Meaning (Contextualized Defin: Describes acting casually, carelessly, or without due seriousness; depending on context it may imply ease, teasing, or criticism.
Usage Contexts: Family teasing; criticism; workplace; storytelling; descriptions of behavior
Cultural Origin or Historical Reference: Attested with the linked meanings “nonchalantly, carefree, nonseriously.” The expression is sociolinguistically sensitive because tone determines whether it sounds approving or reproachful.

Syntactic Structure & Grammatical Form: Fixed focus construction built around a demonstrative/focus element and a residual-necessity expression.
Figurative Meaning (Contextualized Defin: Indicates that only one option, duty, or final step remains; it frames the remaining action as unavoidable or sufficient.
Non-Idiomatic Equivalent (Plain, Neutral: That is the only thing left to do.
Usage Contexts: Planning; problem solving; work; family decisions; narrative turning points
Cultural Origin or Historical Reference: Attested as “the only thing” or “all that’s left to do.” The form packages discourse focus and necessity into a compact conventional expression.
